trials.name: E1900
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed AML, age 17-60, fit for intensive induction
trials.descriptor: Anthracycline dose intensification - daunorubicin 90 vs 45 mg/m2 in 7+3
trials.population: 657 patients aged 17-60 with previously untreated AML
trials.arms: Daunorubicin 90 mg/m2 vs 45 mg/m2 IV daily x 3, each with cytarabine 100 mg/m2/day CIV x 7 days; responders offered allogeneic HCT or HiDAC +/- gemtuzumab then autologous transplant
trials.results: Intention-to-treat: CR 70.6% with high-dose vs 57.3% with standard-dose daunorubicin (P<0.001); median OS 23.7 vs 15.7 months (P=0.003) at median follow-up 25.2 months.
trials.toxicity: Rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups.
trials.reference: Fernandez HF et al. N Engl J Med 2009;361:1249-1259
highlights: Made daunorubicin 90 mg/m2 (or at minimum 60) the standard anthracycline dose in 7+3 for younger adults, displacing 45 mg/m2.
The higher dose bought a better remission rate and longer survival without more serious toxicity - dose intensification is essentially free in a fit patient.
trials.takeaway: Use daunorubicin 90 mg/m2, not 45, with cytarabine in fit adults under 60 - higher CR rate and 8 months longer median survival.

trials.name: ALFA-0701
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed de novo CD33-positive AML, age 50-70, fit for intensive induction
trials.descriptor: Adding fractionated low-dose gemtuzumab ozogamicin to induction and consolidation
trials.population: 280 previously untreated patients aged 50-70 with de novo AML at 26 French centres
trials.arms: Standard induction and consolidation chemotherapy alone vs the same plus fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin 3 mg/m2 IV on days 1, 4 and 7 of induction and day 1 of each of two consolidation courses (five doses total)
trials.toxicity: Persistent thrombocytopenia more common with GO (16% vs 3%; P<0.0001), without an increase in death from toxicity.
highlights: Rehabilitated gemtuzumab after its 2010 market withdrawal by showing that fractionated low doses deliver a higher cumulative dose safely - and drove the 2017 FDA re-approval.
The survival gain concentrates in favourable- and intermediate-risk cytogenetics, which is why GO is routinely added to 7+3 for core-binding-factor AML.
trials.takeaway: Fractionated GO 3 mg/m2 on days 1, 4 and 7 added to 7+3 improves EFS, RFS and OS in CD33-positive AML, at the cost of persistent thrombocytopenia.

trials.name: APL0406
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed low- to intermediate-risk acute promyelocytic leukemia (WBC <=10 x 10^9/L)
trials.descriptor: Chemotherapy-free ATRA + arsenic trioxide versus ATRA + chemotherapy
trials.population: 162 adults with newly diagnosed low-to-intermediate-risk APL; 156 evaluable for response (77 ATRA-ATO, 79 ATRA-chemotherapy)
trials.arms: ATRA + arsenic trioxide for induction and consolidation (chemotherapy-free) vs ATRA-idarubicin induction, three cycles of ATRA + chemotherapy consolidation, and low-dose chemotherapy + ATRA maintenance. Non-inferiority design, 5-point margin for 2-year EFS
trials.results: CR 77/77 (100%) with ATRA-ATO vs 75/79 (95%) with ATRA-chemotherapy (P=0.12). At median follow-up 34.4 months, 2-year EFS 97% vs 86% (95% CI for difference 2-22 points; P<0.001 for non-inferiority, P=0.02 for superiority). Overall survival also better with ATRA-ATO (P=0.02).
trials.toxicity: Less hematologic toxicity and fewer infections with ATRA-ATO, but more hepatic toxicity. QT prolongation and differentiation syndrome are recognized ATO effects, not quantified in the primary report.
trials.reference: Lo-Coco F et al. N Engl J Med 2013;369:111-121
highlights: Established a completely chemotherapy-free regimen as standard of care for non-high-risk APL, with cure rates above 95% and no anthracycline exposure.
Trades myelosuppression and infection for hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation and differentiation syndrome - a monitorable rather than life-threatening profile in most patients.
trials.takeaway: For low/intermediate-risk APL, ATRA + arsenic trioxide is non-inferior and probably superior to ATRA + chemotherapy, and spares cytotoxics entirely.

trials.name: MRC/NCRI AML15
trials.setting: Younger adults with newly diagnosed AML, consolidation phase
trials.descriptor: Multi-randomization trial; the consolidation question was cytarabine 1.5 vs 3 g/m2
trials.population: Younger AML patients, median age 49 (range 0-73); the cytarabine consolidation dose comparison included 657 patients
trials.arms: Cytarabine consolidation 3 g/m2 vs 1.5 g/m2 (n=657). Other randomizations in the same trial: DA +/- etoposide; ADE vs FLAG-Ida; MACE-MidAc vs high-dose cytarabine; a fifth course or not
trials.primary_endpoint: Not designated in the primary report; outcomes reported are remission rate, relapse, relapse-free survival and overall survival
trials.results: Cytarabine 1.5 g/m2 was equivalent to 3 g/m2 - no benefit from dose escalation (no HR or p-value published for this comparison). Outcomes were similar between MACE/MidAc and high-dose cytarabine, but cytarabine required less supportive care; MACE/MidAc was superior for high-risk patients; a fifth course provided no benefit. For FLAG-Ida x2 plus cytarabine x2, 8-year survival was 63% (intermediate risk) and 95% (favourable risk).
trials.toxicity: No toxicity difference reported between the 1.5 and 3 g/m2 cytarabine doses.
trials.reference: Burnett AK et al. J Clin Oncol 2013;31:3360-3368
highlights: The randomized evidence that intermediate-dose cytarabine (1.5 g/m2) consolidation is equivalent to high-dose (3 g/m2), underpinning the widespread use of lower-dose schedules - particularly relevant over age 60.
A factorial multi-randomization trial that also showed no benefit from a fifth chemotherapy course and defined FLAG-Ida as effective induction for younger adults.
trials.takeaway: Escalating consolidation cytarabine from 1.5 to 3 g/m2 adds nothing - the lower dose is equivalent.

trials.name: RATIFY (CALGB 10603)
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed FLT3-mutated AML, age 18-59, fit for intensive induction
trials.descriptor: Adding midostaurin to 7+3 induction, consolidation and maintenance
trials.population: 717 FLT3-mutated patients aged 18-59 with newly diagnosed non-APL AML (ITD-high 214, ITD-low 341, TKD 162), screened from 3277; 68.6% normal karyotype
trials.arms: Midostaurin 50 mg PO BID days 8-21 vs placebo, each added to daunorubicin 60 mg/m2 days 1-3 + cytarabine 200 mg/m2 CIV days 1-7; then 4 cycles HiDAC 3000 mg/m2 q12h days 1, 3, 5; then 12 cycles maintenance
trials.results: Median OS 74.7 months (95% CI 31.5-NR) vs 25.6 months (95% CI 18.6-42.9); HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.96), one-sided P=0.009. 4-year OS 51.4% vs 44.3%. Median EFS 8.2 vs 3.0 months, HR 0.78 (0.66-0.93), P=0.002. CR 58.9% vs 53.5% (P=0.15). Benefit consistent across ITD-high, ITD-low and TKD and in the transplant-censored analysis; 57.0% underwent transplant.
trials.toxicity: Similar overall severe adverse events; grade 3-5 rash higher with midostaurin (14.1% vs 7.6%, P=0.008) and anemia (92.7% vs 87.8%, P=0.03).
trials.reference: Stone RM et al. N Engl J Med 2017;377:454-464
highlights: The first targeted agent to improve survival when added to 7+3, and the trial that made rapid FLT3 testing at diagnosis mandatory - the inhibitor starts on day 8.
Benefit held across ITD-high, ITD-low and TKD, so midostaurin is given for any activating FLT3 mutation, not ITD alone.
trials.takeaway: Add midostaurin to 7+3 and consolidation for any FLT3-mutated AML in a fit younger adult - 22% lower risk of death.

trials.name: CPX-351 (Study 301)
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed high-risk or secondary AML, age 60-75, fit for intensive induction
trials.descriptor: Liposomal cytarabine-daunorubicin (5:1 fixed ratio) versus conventional 7+3
trials.population: 309 patients age 60-75 with newly diagnosed high-risk or secondary AML
trials.arms: CPX-351 (dual-drug liposomal cytarabine + daunorubicin, 5:1 molar ratio) vs conventional 7+3; one to two induction cycles followed by similar consolidation
trials.results: Median OS 9.56 vs 5.95 months; HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.52-0.90), one-sided P=.003. Overall remission rate 47.7% vs 33.3% (two-sided P=.016). Improvements seen across age groups and AML subtypes. Early mortality: day 30 5.9% vs 10.6% (P=.149); day 60 13.7% vs 21.2% (P=.097).
trials.toxicity: Non-hematologic adverse event rates comparable between arms, but prolonged time to neutrophil and platelet recovery with CPX-351 and a longer treatment phase.
trials.reference: Lancet JE et al. J Clin Oncol 2018;36:2684-2692
highlights: The trial that established CPX-351 for secondary and therapy-related AML in older adults, and the basis for its FDA approval.

Important caveat: the comparator was 7+3, not venetoclax + azacitidine. Real-world survival is comparable to ven/aza, so the niche has narrowed to the fitter older adult (~60-75) with secondary or therapy-related AML who is a transplant candidate.
trials.takeaway: CPX-351 beat 7+3 on survival in older adults with secondary or high-risk AML (9.56 vs 5.95 months), but it was never compared with venetoclax + azacitidine.

trials.name: ADMIRAL
trials.descriptor: Single-agent gilteritinib versus investigator-choice salvage chemotherapy
trials.population: 371 eligible adults with relapsed or refractory FLT3-mutated AML
trials.arms: Gilteritinib 120 mg PO daily (n=247) vs salvage chemotherapy (n=124), randomized 2:1
trials.primary_endpoint: Dual: overall survival, and complete remission with full or partial hematologic recovery (CR/CRh)
trials.results: Median OS 9.3 vs 5.6 months; HR 0.64 (95% CI 0.49-0.83), P<0.001. CR/CRh 34.0% vs 15.3% (difference 18.6 points, 95% CI 9.8-27.4); CR 21.1% vs 10.5%. Median EFS 2.8 vs 0.7 months; HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.58-1.09).
trials.toxicity: Adjusted for therapy duration, grade >=3 and serious adverse events were less frequent with gilteritinib. Most common grade >=3 with gilteritinib: febrile neutropenia 45.9%, anemia 40.7%, thrombocytopenia 22.8%. Differentiation syndrome and QT prolongation are class effects.
trials.reference: Perl AE et al. N Engl J Med 2019;381:1728-1740
highlights: Made single-agent gilteritinib the standard salvage for relapsed/refractory FLT3-mutated AML, beating intensive chemotherapy on survival with less toxicity.
An oral, better-tolerated bridge to allogeneic transplant - the higher CR/CRh rate translates into more patients actually reaching transplant.
trials.takeaway: In relapsed/refractory FLT3-mutated AML, oral gilteritinib beats salvage chemotherapy on survival (9.3 vs 5.6 months) with fewer severe toxicities.

trials.name: QUAZAR AML-001
trials.setting: AML in first complete remission after intensive induction, age 55+, not a transplant candidate
trials.descriptor: Oral azacitidine (CC-486) maintenance versus placebo in CR1
trials.population: 472 patients aged >=55 in complete remission with or without count recovery after intensive chemotherapy, not candidates for stem-cell transplantation; median age 68
trials.arms: CC-486 (oral azacitidine, NOT bioequivalent to injectable azacitidine) 300 mg PO daily for 14 days of each 28-day cycle (n=238) vs placebo (n=234)
trials.results: Median OS from randomization 24.7 vs 14.8 months (P<0.001; HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55-0.86). Median relapse-free survival 10.2 vs 4.8 months (P<0.001). Benefit across most baseline subgroups; health-related quality of life preserved.
trials.toxicity: Most common events grade 1-2 gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). Grade 3-4 neutropenia 41% vs 24%; thrombocytopenia 22% vs 21%.
trials.reference: Wei AH et al. N Engl J Med 2020;383:2526-2537
highlights: Created a maintenance standard for older AML patients in CR1 who cannot proceed to transplant - the first maintenance strategy to prolong overall survival in this setting.
CC-486 is a distinct oral formulation and is NOT interchangeable with injectable azacitidine; 300 mg for 14 days per cycle is the tested schedule.
trials.takeaway: Oral azacitidine 300 mg for 14 days per cycle as CR1 maintenance adds about 10 months of median overall survival in older AML patients who are not transplant candidates.

trials.name: VIALE-A
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed AML ineligible for intensive induction (age 75+ or significant comorbidity)
trials.descriptor: Adding venetoclax to azacitidine in unfit newly diagnosed AML
trials.population: 431 previously untreated patients ineligible for standard induction because of coexisting conditions, age >=75, or both; median age 76
trials.arms: Azacitidine 75 mg/m2 SC or IV days 1-7 of each 28-day cycle plus venetoclax (target 400 mg) PO daily (n=286) or placebo (n=145)
trials.results: At median follow-up 20.5 months, median OS 14.7 vs 9.6 months; HR 0.66 (95% CI 0.52-0.85), P<0.001. CR 36.7% vs 17.9% (P<0.001); composite CR 66.4% vs 28.3% (P<0.001).
trials.toxicity: Grade >=3 febrile neutropenia 42% vs 19%; thrombocytopenia 45% vs 38%; neutropenia 42% vs 28%; any-grade infection 85% vs 67%; serious adverse events 83% vs 73%.
trials.reference: DiNardo CD et al. N Engl J Med 2020;383:617-629
highlights: Redefined frontline therapy for AML unfit for induction, roughly doubling the CR rate and adding 5 months of median survival over a hypomethylating agent alone.
The cost is real myelosuppression - febrile neutropenia more than doubled - so cycle-1 marrow assessment, venetoclax duration truncation and azole dose adjustment are part of delivering it safely.
trials.takeaway: Azacitidine + venetoclax is standard for newly diagnosed AML unfit for intensive chemotherapy: median OS 14.7 vs 9.6 months.

trials.name: AGILE
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML, ineligible for intensive induction
trials.descriptor: Adding the IDH1 inhibitor ivosidenib to azacitidine
trials.population: 146 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML ineligible for intensive induction (72 ivosidenib-azacitidine, 74 placebo-azacitidine)
trials.arms: Ivosidenib 500 mg PO daily + azacitidine 75 mg/m2 for 7 days of each 28-day cycle vs placebo + the same azacitidine
trials.primary_endpoint: Event-free survival (treatment failure, relapse or death)
trials.results: At median follow-up 12.4 months, HR for treatment failure, relapse or death 0.33 (95% CI 0.16-0.69), P=0.002; event-free at 12 months 37% vs 12%. Median OS 24.0 vs 7.9 months; HR 0.44 (95% CI 0.27-0.73), P=0.001.
trials.toxicity: Grade >=3 febrile neutropenia 28% vs 34%, neutropenia 27% vs 16%; any-grade bleeding 41% vs 29%; infection 28% vs 49%. Differentiation syndrome any grade 14% vs 8%.
trials.reference: Montesinos P et al. N Engl J Med 2022;386:1519-1531
highlights: Established ivosidenib + azacitidine as a frontline option for IDH1-mutated AML unfit for induction, with a median OS of 24 months - the longest reported in this population.
Interpret the EFS with care: failure to achieve CR by week 24 counted as an event dated back to randomization, which inflates early curve separation. The OS result is the more robust finding.
trials.takeaway: In IDH1-mutant AML unfit for induction, ivosidenib + azacitidine triples median overall survival (24.0 vs 7.9 months); watch for differentiation syndrome.

trials.name: QuANTUM-First
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive AML, age 18-75, fit for intensive induction
trials.descriptor: Adding the type II FLT3 inhibitor quizartinib to 7+3, consolidation and up to 3 years of continuation
trials.population: 539 adults aged 18-75 with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive AML at 193 sites in 26 countries; median age 56
trials.arms: Quizartinib 40 mg PO daily from day 8 for 14 days vs placebo, added to standard 7+3; responders received HiDAC consolidation with quizartinib or placebo, allogeneic HCT, or both, then single-agent continuation up to 3 years
trials.results: At median follow-up 39.2 months, median OS 31.9 months (95% CI 21.0-NE) vs 15.1 months (95% CI 13.2-26.2); HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.62-0.98), P=0.032.
trials.toxicity: Grade >=3 adverse events 92% vs 90%; most common febrile neutropenia, hypokalaemia and pneumonia in both arms, plus neutropenia with quizartinib. Known QT-prolongation risk drives the REMS requirement.
highlights: A second FLT3 inhibitor option for newly diagnosed disease, doubling median overall survival versus chemotherapy alone in FLT3-ITD AML.
Unlike RATIFY it enrolled up to age 75 and included up to 3 years of continuation - but it applies only to ITD-positive disease, since quizartinib has no activity against TKD mutations.
trials.takeaway: Quizartinib added to 7+3 prolongs survival in FLT3-ITD AML up to age 75, with QT monitoring as the practical cost.

trials.name: SWOG S1203
trials.setting: Newly diagnosed AML in younger adults, fit for intensive induction
trials.descriptor: Standard 7+3 versus idarubicin/high-dose cytarabine, with or without vorinostat
trials.population: 738 eligible younger adults with newly diagnosed AML registered 2013-2015; APL and CML blast phase excluded
trials.arms: DA (7+3): daunorubicin 90 mg/m2 + cytarabine 100 mg/m2/day CIV (n=261). IA: idarubicin 12 mg/m2 x3 + cytarabine 1500 mg/m2/day CIV x4 days (n=261). IA+V: vorinostat 500 mg PO TID days 1-3 then IA (n=216; stopped early for futility)
trials.primary_endpoint: Event-free survival (DA vs IA or IA+V); overall survival was secondary
trials.results: No arm beat 7+3. Overall response 77.5% (CR 62.5%, CRi 15.0%) with no difference between arms. At median follow-up 33 months, no significant EFS difference (all P>0.38): 2-year EFS 36% / 41% / 37%. No significant OS difference (all P>0.29): 2-year OS 57% / 59% / 57%. In favourable cytogenetics DA was significantly BETTER than IA (P=0.008) and IA+V (P=0.006). IA+V closed for futility at the second interim analysis; IA later crossed a futility boundary.
trials.toxicity: More toxicity in the experimental arms, driven by IA+V: grade 3 diarrhea 6%/8%/18% (P<0.001); grade 3 typhlitis 3%/5%/10% (P=0.002); grade 4 sepsis 6%/7%/13% (P=0.002); grade 5 sepsis 0%/3%/3% (P=0.03).
highlights: A negative trial that settled the question: high-dose cytarabine induction, with or without vorinostat, does not improve remission, EFS or OS over standard 7+3, and adds gastrointestinal and infectious toxicity.
In favourable-risk cytogenetics the experimental regimens were actually worse than 7+3, reinforcing DA plus gemtuzumab as the right backbone for core-binding-factor AML.
trials.takeaway: 7+3 remains the standard induction for fit younger adults - idarubicin/high-dose cytarabine, with or without vorinostat, offered no benefit and more toxicity.

trials.name: NSABP B-24
trials.descriptor: tamoxifen after lumpectomy and radiation for DCIS
trials.population: DCIS treated with lumpectomy + whole-breast radiation (positive margins allowed)
trials.arms: Tamoxifen 20 mg/day × 5 years vs placebo
trials.results: Breast-cancer events at 5 yr 8.2% vs 13.4% (p=0.0009); cumulative invasive events 4.1% at 5 yr with tamoxifen (2.1% ipsilateral, 1.8% contralateral); benefit seen even with involved margins; later analysis showed the benefit is confined to ER-positive DCIS (Allred, JCO 2012)
trials.toxicity: Endometrial cancer, VTE, hot flashes
trials.reference: Fisher B et al. Lancet 1999;353:1993; Allred DC et al. JCO 2012;30:1268 (ER subset)
highlights: Tamoxifen after BCS + RT for ER-positive DCIS reduces both ipsilateral and contralateral events; no survival benefit, so it is a shared decision.
Test ER on DCIS — ER-negative DCIS gains nothing.
trials.takeaway: Tamoxifen reduces ipsilateral and contralateral breast events after lumpectomy + RT for ER+ DCIS

trials.name: ACOSOG Z0011
trials.descriptor: sentinel node biopsy alone vs completion axillary dissection
trials.population: cT1–2 N0 breast cancer with 1–2 positive sentinel nodes, treated with lumpectomy + whole-breast RT
trials.arms: Sentinel lymph node dissection alone vs completion axillary lymph node dissection
trials.results: 5-yr OS 92.5% vs 91.8% (SLND alone vs ALND; HR 0.79) and 5-yr DFS 83.9% vs 82.2% — non-inferior; 10-yr update: OS 86.3% vs 83.6%, DFS 80.2% vs 78.2%, regional recurrence 1.5% vs 0.5%
trials.toxicity: Lymphedema, wound infection, paresthesia markedly lower without ALND
trials.reference: Giuliano AE et al. JAMA 2011;305:569; JAMA 2017;318:918 (10-yr)
highlights: Completion ALND is unnecessary for 1–2 positive sentinel nodes after lumpectomy with whole-breast RT — tangent fields cover the low axilla.
Does not apply to mastectomy without RT, ≥3 positive nodes, matted nodes, or node-positive after neoadjuvant therapy.
trials.takeaway: SLNB alone is non-inferior to ALND for 1–2 positive sentinel nodes with lumpectomy + RT

trials.name: SOFT
trials.descriptor: ovarian suppression added to tamoxifen or exemestane, premenopausal
trials.population: Premenopausal HR+ early breast cancer (remaining premenopausal after chemo, if given)
trials.arms: Tamoxifen alone vs tamoxifen + ovarian suppression vs exemestane + ovarian suppression (× 5 years)
trials.results: Primary (5-yr): DFS 86.6% vs 84.7% (HR 0.83, NS overall); in women who had chemotherapy 82.5% vs 78.0% (HR 0.78). 8-yr update: DFS 83.2% vs 78.9% (HR 0.76), OS 93.3% vs 91.5%; exemestane + OFS 8-yr DFS 85.9%. Largest benefit in women <35 and those needing chemotherapy
trials.toxicity: Menopausal symptoms, osteoporosis, depression, hypertension, sexual dysfunction with OFS
trials.reference: Francis PA et al. NEJM 2015;372:436; NEJM 2018;379:122 (8-yr, with TEXT)
highlights: Add ovarian suppression for premenopausal women at high enough risk to warrant chemotherapy; tamoxifen alone remains reasonable for low-risk disease.
Exemestane + OFS gives the best DFS but not OS; toxicity and adherence limit its use.
trials.takeaway: Ovarian suppression added to tamoxifen improves DFS in higher-risk premenopausal HR+ breast cancer

trials.name: CREATE-X
trials.descriptor: adjuvant capecitabine after residual disease, HER2-negative
trials.population: HER2-negative breast cancer with residual invasive disease after neoadjuvant anthracycline/taxane chemotherapy (Japan/Korea)
trials.arms: Capecitabine 1250 mg/m² BID d1–14 q3wk × 6–8 cycles vs no further chemotherapy (both with standard endocrine/RT)
trials.toxicity: Hand-foot syndrome (73%), neutropenia, diarrhea
highlights: Residual TNBC after neoadjuvant chemo → adjuvant capecitabine × 6–8 cycles; the benefit in HR+ disease was small.
Asian population and 1250 mg/m² dosing; US practice often uses 1000 mg/m² BID for tolerability.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant capecitabine improves DFS and OS for residual disease after neoadjuvant chemo, mostly in TNBC

trials.name: TAILORx
trials.descriptor: Oncotype DX RS 11–25: endocrine therapy alone vs chemo-endocrine
trials.population: HR+/HER2−, node-negative breast cancer (1.1–5 cm or 0.6–1 cm high grade); RS 11–25 randomized; RS ≤10 endocrine only, RS ≥26 chemo-endocrine
trials.arms: Endocrine therapy alone vs chemotherapy + endocrine therapy (RS 11–25)
trials.results: 9-yr iDFS 83.3% vs 84.3% (HR 1.08) — endocrine alone non-inferior. Women ≤50 with RS 16–25 had a 6–7 point iDFS benefit from chemo; RS ≤10 9-yr distant recurrence 3%
trials.reference: Sparano JA et al. NEJM 2018;379:111; NEJM 2015;373:2005 (RS ≤10)
highlights: Chemotherapy can be omitted for RS ≤25 in node-negative disease if age >50; in women ≤50, RS 16–25 still favors chemotherapy (possibly via ovarian suppression).
RS ≥26 → chemotherapy; RS ≤10 → endocrine therapy alone regardless of age.
trials.takeaway: Endocrine therapy alone is non-inferior for RS 11–25 node-negative HR+ disease, except women ≤50 with RS 16–25

trials.name: KATHERINE
trials.descriptor: T-DM1 vs trastuzumab for residual invasive disease after neoadjuvant therapy
trials.population: HER2+ early breast cancer with residual invasive disease in breast or axilla after neoadjuvant taxane + trastuzumab
trials.arms: Trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) 3.6 mg/kg q3wk × 14 vs trastuzumab × 14
trials.toxicity: Thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, peripheral neuropathy; more discontinuation with T-DM1 (18% vs 2%)
trials.reference: von Minckwitz G et al. NEJM 2019;380:617; Geyer CE et al. NEJM 2025 (OS)
highlights: Residual disease after neoadjuvant HER2 therapy → switch to T-DM1 × 14 rather than completing trastuzumab.
The main argument for neoadjuvant therapy in HER2+ disease: response guides escalation.
trials.takeaway: T-DM1 halves recurrence risk for HER2+ residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy

trials.name: HER2CLIMB
trials.descriptor: tucatinib + trastuzumab + capecitabine, previously treated HER2+ metastatic
trials.population: HER2+ metastatic breast cancer after trastuzumab, pertuzumab and T-DM1; active or stable brain metastases allowed (~48% had brain mets)
trials.arms: Tucatinib 300 mg BID + trastuzumab + capecitabine vs placebo + trastuzumab + capecitabine
trials.results: 1-yr PFS 33.1% vs 12.3%, median 7.8 vs 5.6 mo (HR 0.54); OS 21.9 vs 17.4 mo (HR 0.66; updated 24.7 vs 19.2, HR 0.73); brain metastases: 1-yr PFS 24.9% vs 0%, median 7.6 vs 5.4 mo (HR 0.48); CNS-PFS 9.9 vs 4.2 mo (HR 0.32, Lin JCO 2020)
trials.toxicity: Diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome, transaminase elevation
trials.reference: Murthy RK et al. NEJM 2020;382:597; Lin NU et al. JCO 2020 (CNS); Curigliano G et al. Ann Oncol 2022 (OS)
highlights: The only HER2 regimen with an OS benefit in patients with active brain metastases — tucatinib is the go-to for HER2+ CNS disease.
Tucatinib is HER2-selective (spares EGFR) → less diarrhea/rash than neratinib or lapatinib.
trials.takeaway: Tucatinib + trastuzumab + capecitabine improves PFS and OS in pretreated HER2+ disease, including active brain metastases

trials.name: KEYNOTE-522
trials.descriptor: neoadjuvant pembrolizumab + chemo → adjuvant pembrolizumab, early TNBC
trials.population: Previously untreated stage II–III triple-negative breast cancer (T1c N1–2 or T2–4 N0–2), regardless of PD-L1
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab + carboplatin/paclitaxel → pembrolizumab + AC/EC, then adjuvant pembrolizumab × 9 cycles, vs placebo + the same chemotherapy
trials.primary_endpoint: Pathologic complete response (ypT0/Tis ypN0) and event-free survival
trials.toxicity: Immune-mediated AEs (thyroid dysfunction, adrenal insufficiency, pneumonitis); grade ≥3 AEs ~78% both arms
trials.reference: Schmid P et al. NEJM 2020;382:810 (pCR); NEJM 2022;386:556 (EFS); NEJM 2024;391:1981 (OS)
highlights: The standard for stage ≥II TNBC: pembrolizumab with neoadjuvant chemo, continued adjuvantly regardless of pCR.
Benefit independent of PD-L1 status — do not test CPS to select early-stage patients (unlike metastatic TNBC).
trials.takeaway: Pembrolizumab + chemo neoadjuvant then adjuvant improves pCR, EFS and OS in stage II–III TNBC

trials.name: monarchE
trials.descriptor: adjuvant abemaciclib × 2 years, node-positive high-risk HR+/HER2−
trials.population: HR+/HER2− early breast cancer, node-positive high risk: ≥4 positive nodes, or 1–3 nodes plus grade 3, tumor ≥5 cm, or Ki-67 ≥20%
trials.arms: Abemaciclib 150 mg BID × 2 years + endocrine therapy vs endocrine therapy alone
trials.results: 2-yr iDFS 92.2% vs 88.7% (HR 0.75) at primary analysis; 4-yr iDFS 85.8% vs 79.4% (HR 0.66); 5-yr iDFS 83.6% vs 76.0% — benefit deepens after abemaciclib stops; OS immature
trials.toxicity: Diarrhea (84%, mostly grade 1–2), neutropenia, fatigue, VTE (2.5%), ILD (rare)
trials.reference: Johnston SRD et al. JCO 2020;38:3987; Lancet Oncol 2023;24:77 (4-yr); Rastogi P et al. JCO 2024 (5-yr)
highlights: The first CDK4/6 inhibitor to succeed in the adjuvant setting (PALLAS and PENELOPE-B with palbociclib were negative).
Two-year course; the absolute benefit keeps widening after treatment ends (carry-over effect).
trials.takeaway: 2 years of adjuvant abemaciclib improves iDFS in node-positive high-risk HR+/HER2− breast cancer

trials.name: OlympiA
trials.descriptor: adjuvant olaparib × 1 year, germline BRCA-mutated HER2-negative
trials.population: Germline BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant, HER2-negative, high-risk early breast cancer (TNBC with residual disease or ≥pT2/pN1; HR+ with residual disease and CPS+EG ≥3 or ≥4 nodes) after (neo)adjuvant chemo
trials.arms: Olaparib 300 mg BID × 1 year vs placebo
trials.toxicity: Anemia, nausea, fatigue; no excess MDS/AML at 3.5 yr
trials.reference: Tutt ANJ et al. NEJM 2021;384:2394; Geyer CE et al. Ann Oncol 2022 (OS)
highlights: Germline BRCA testing now has an adjuvant treatment consequence — test all TNBC and high-risk HER2− patients eligible by NCCN/ASCO criteria.
One year of olaparib after chemotherapy; sequencing with pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-522) or endocrine therapy is extrapolated.
trials.takeaway: 1 year of adjuvant olaparib improves iDFS and OS in high-risk gBRCA HER2-negative breast cancer

trials.name: RxPONDER
trials.descriptor: Oncotype DX RS ≤25 with 1–3 positive nodes: chemo benefit by menopausal status
trials.population: HR+/HER2− breast cancer with 1–3 positive axillary nodes and Recurrence Score ≤25
trials.arms: Endocrine therapy alone vs chemotherapy + endocrine therapy
trials.results: Postmenopausal: 5-yr iDFS 91.9% vs 91.3% — no chemotherapy benefit. Premenopausal: 5-yr iDFS 93.9% vs 89.0% (HR 0.60), OS 98.6% vs 97.3%
highlights: Postmenopausal women with 1–3 nodes and RS ≤25 can skip chemotherapy; premenopausal women still benefit (unclear whether from cytotoxicity or chemo-induced ovarian suppression).
Extends genomic-assay-driven de-escalation into node-positive disease.
trials.takeaway: With 1–3 nodes and RS ≤25, chemo adds nothing postmenopausally but still benefits premenopausal women

trials.name: MAINTAIN
trials.descriptor: switch to ribociclib + alternative endocrine therapy after CDK4/6 progression
trials.population: HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer progressing on a CDK4/6 inhibitor + endocrine therapy (86% prior palbociclib)
trials.arms: Ribociclib + switched endocrine therapy (fulvestrant or exemestane) vs placebo + switched endocrine therapy
highlights: First randomized evidence that continuing CDK4/6 blockade (with a switch of agent and endocrine partner) beyond progression has value.
Modest absolute benefit; genomic-driven options (PIK3CA, ESR1, AKT/PTEN) take priority when a target exists.
trials.takeaway: Ribociclib + switched endocrine therapy after CDK4/6i progression modestly improves PFS

trials.name: SOUND
trials.setting: Surgery, small tumor, negative axillary ultrasound
trials.descriptor: omission of sentinel node biopsy with negative axillary ultrasound
trials.population: Breast cancer ≤2 cm with negative preoperative axillary ultrasound, planned breast conservation + RT
trials.arms: Sentinel lymph node biopsy vs no axillary surgery
trials.results: 5-yr DDFS 97.7% vs 98.0% (HR 0.84) — non-inferior; nodal positivity in the SLNB arm was 13.7%, yet outcomes were unaffected
trials.reference: Gentilini OD et al. JAMA Oncol 2023;9:1557
highlights: Axillary staging can be omitted for small, clinically node-negative tumors with a negative ultrasound — especially in older, HR+ patients where nodal status won't change systemic therapy.
Missed nodal disease had no measurable impact because adjuvant decisions were driven by tumor biology.
trials.takeaway: Omitting SLNB is non-inferior for tumors ≤2 cm with negative axillary ultrasound

trials.name: NATALEE
trials.descriptor: adjuvant ribociclib × 3 years, stage II–III HR+/HER2− incl. node-negative
trials.population: HR+/HER2− early breast cancer: any stage III, stage IIB, or stage IIA with grade 3 or grade 2 with high genomic risk/Ki-67 ≥20% (node-negative allowed)
trials.arms: Ribociclib 400 mg daily 3 wk on/1 off × 3 years + NSAI (± ovarian suppression) vs NSAI alone
trials.results: 3-yr iDFS 90.4% vs 87.1% (HR 0.75); 4-yr iDFS 88.5% vs 83.6% (HR 0.72); OS immature
trials.toxicity: Neutropenia, arthralgia, LFT elevation; QTc prolongation (400 mg dose lowers this vs 600 mg)
trials.reference: Slamon D et al. NEJM 2024;390:1080; Fasching PA et al. Ann Oncol 2025 (4-yr)
highlights: Broadens adjuvant CDK4/6 eligibility to node-negative stage II disease, at a lower 400 mg dose for 3 years.
Absolute benefit is ~3–5 points; discuss duration, cost and toxicity against monarchE's 2-year regimen when both qualify.
trials.takeaway: 3 years of adjuvant ribociclib improves iDFS in stage II–III HR+/HER2− breast cancer including node-negative

trials.name: postMONARCH
trials.descriptor: abemaciclib + fulvestrant after progression on CDK4/6 inhibitor + AI
trials.population: HR+/HER2− advanced breast cancer progressing on a CDK4/6 inhibitor + aromatase inhibitor (metastatic or adjuvant)
trials.arms: Abemaciclib + fulvestrant vs placebo + fulvestrant
trials.results: PFS 6.0 vs 5.3 mo (HR 0.73); ORR 17% vs 7%; consistent across prior CDK4/6i and ESR1/PIK3CA status
trials.reference: Kalinsky K et al. JCO 2025;43:1101 (ASCO 2024 LBA1001)
highlights: Phase 3 confirmation of the MAINTAIN concept with abemaciclib; the absolute gain is small (~0.7 mo median) but the HR is meaningful.
Reasonable option when no actionable alteration is present and the patient tolerates CDK4/6 inhibition.
trials.takeaway: Abemaciclib + fulvestrant modestly improves PFS after CDK4/6 inhibitor progression

trials.name: OPTIMOX1
trials.descriptor: stop-and-go oxaliplatin to limit neuropathy
trials.population: Untreated metastatic colorectal cancer
trials.arms: FOLFOX4 until progression vs FOLFOX7 × 6 → sFU/LV maintenance × 12 → FOLFOX7 reintroduction
trials.results: PFS 9.0 vs 8.7 mo and OS 19.3 vs 21.2 mo (NS); response 58.5% vs 59.2%; grade 3 neuropathy 17.9% vs 13.3%; oxaliplatin reintroduced in only 40% but achieved response or stabilization in 69% of them
highlights: Oxaliplatin can be stopped after ~3–4 months and reintroduced without losing efficacy — the basis for planned oxaliplatin holidays in metastatic disease.
OPTIMOX2 later showed that stopping all chemotherapy (complete break) is worse than fluoropyrimidine maintenance.
trials.takeaway: Planned oxaliplatin stop-and-go preserves efficacy and limits neuropathy in metastatic CRC

trials.name: TRIBE
trials.descriptor: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab vs FOLFIRI + bevacizumab
trials.population: Untreated unresectable metastatic colorectal cancer, age ≤75, ECOG ≤2 (≤1 if 71–75)
trials.arms: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab vs FOLFIRI + bevacizumab (induction × 12, then 5-FU/bev maintenance)
trials.results: PFS 12.1 vs 9.7 mo (HR 0.75); ORR 65% vs 53%; OS 31.0 vs 25.8 mo (HR 0.79, p=0.054; updated 29.8 vs 25.8, HR 0.80). BRAF-mutant: OS 19.0 vs 10.7 mo (n=28)
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 neutropenia 50% vs 20%, diarrhea 19% vs 11%, neuropathy 5% vs 0%
trials.reference: Loupakis F et al. NEJM 2014;371:1609; Cremolini C et al. Lancet Oncol 2015 (OS)
highlights: Triplet chemotherapy + bevacizumab improves PFS, ORR and OS for fit patients — favored for right-sided or RAS-mutant disease and when downsizing matters.
Toxicity limits it to fit patients ≤75; the BRAF signal was hypothesis-generating and superseded by BREAKWATER.
trials.takeaway: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab improves PFS, response and OS over FOLFIRI + bevacizumab in fit patients

trials.name: IDEA collaboration
trials.descriptor: 3 vs 6 months of adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy
trials.population: Stage III colon cancer after resection (pooled analysis of 6 randomized trials)
trials.arms: 3 months vs 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX (regimen chosen by investigator)
trials.results: 3-yr DFS 74.6% vs 75.5% (HR 1.07) — failed non-inferiority overall. CAPOX: 3 mo non-inferior (HR 0.95); FOLFOX: 6 mo better (HR 1.16). Low-risk (T1–3 N1): 3 mo non-inferior; high-risk (T4 or N2): 6 mo favored
trials.toxicity: Grade ≥2 neuropathy 16.6% (3 mo) vs 47.7% (6 mo)
highlights: 3 months of CAPOX is acceptable for low-risk stage III (T1–3 N1); FOLFOX or high-risk disease (T4 and/or N2) favors 6 months.
Neuropathy is the currency — 6 months triples persistent oxaliplatin neuropathy.
trials.takeaway: 3 months of adjuvant CAPOX is non-inferior for low-risk stage III; FOLFOX and high-risk disease favor 6 months

trials.name: BEACON CRC
trials.descriptor: encorafenib + cetuximab ± binimetinib after prior therapy, BRAF V600E
trials.population: BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic CRC after 1–2 prior regimens
trials.arms: Encorafenib + binimetinib + cetuximab (triplet) vs encorafenib + cetuximab (doublet) vs irinotecan/FOLFIRI + cetuximab (control)
trials.results: Primary: OS triplet 9.0 vs control 5.4 mo (HR 0.52); doublet 8.4 mo (HR 0.60); ORR 26% / 20% / 2%. Updated (JCO 2021): OS 9.3 / 9.3 / 5.9 mo. Doublet became the approved standard (MEK adds toxicity, not survival)
trials.toxicity: Diarrhea, dermatitis acneiform, nausea; more GI/ocular toxicity with binimetinib
trials.reference: Kopetz S et al. NEJM 2019;381:1632; JCO 2021 (updated)
highlights: First targeted regimen to improve OS in BRAF V600E CRC — BRAF inhibition needs EGFR blockade (feedback reactivation), unlike melanoma.
Now the second-line option after BREAKWATER took the combination first line.
trials.takeaway: Encorafenib + cetuximab improves OS vs chemo in previously treated BRAF V600E metastatic CRC

trials.name: KEYNOTE-177
trials.descriptor: first-line pembrolizumab vs chemotherapy, MSI-H metastatic CRC
trials.population: Untreated MSI-H/dMMR metastatic colorectal cancer
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab 200 mg q3wk vs investigator's-choice chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab or cetuximab); crossover allowed
trials.results: PFS 16.5 vs 8.2 mo (HR 0.60); ORR 43.8% vs 33.1%; OS HR 0.74 (NS, 60% crossover); 5-yr OS 54.8% vs 44.2%
trials.toxicity: Grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs 22% vs 66%
trials.reference: André T et al. NEJM 2020;383:2207; Diaz LA et al. Lancet Oncol 2022 (OS)
highlights: Pembrolizumab is the first-line standard for MSI-H metastatic CRC — doubles PFS with far less toxicity.
Note early crossover of curves: ~30% progress early on pembrolizumab; chemo-first is reasonable if rapid control is needed.
trials.takeaway: First-line pembrolizumab doubles PFS in MSI-H metastatic colorectal cancer

trials.name: ATOMIC (Alliance A021502)
trials.descriptor: atezolizumab added to adjuvant FOLFOX, stage III dMMR
trials.population: Resected stage III dMMR/MSI-H colon cancer
trials.arms: mFOLFOX6 × 12 + atezolizumab (during and 6 months after chemo) vs mFOLFOX6 × 12
trials.reference: Sinicrope FA et al. ASCO 2025 LBA1; NEJM 2025
highlights: First positive adjuvant immunotherapy trial in colon cancer — dMMR stage III now gets FOLFOX + atezolizumab.
Test MMR/MSI on every newly diagnosed colon cancer; it now changes adjuvant therapy, not just metastatic.
trials.takeaway: Adding atezolizumab to adjuvant FOLFOX halves recurrence risk in stage III dMMR colon cancer

trials.name: BREAKWATER
trials.descriptor: encorafenib + cetuximab + mFOLFOX6 first-line, BRAF V600E metastatic CRC
trials.population: Untreated BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer
trials.arms: Encorafenib + cetuximab + mFOLFOX6 vs encorafenib + cetuximab vs standard chemotherapy ± bevacizumab
trials.results: ORR 60.9% vs 40.0% (triplet+chemo vs control); median OS 30.3 vs 15.1 mo (HR 0.49); PFS 12.8 vs 7.1 mo (HR 0.53)
trials.toxicity: Neutropenia, nausea, anemia, dermatologic (cetuximab)
trials.reference: Kopetz S et al. Nat Med 2025 (ORR); Elez E et al. NEJM 2025 (PFS/OS); FDA accelerated approval Dec 2024
highlights: Moved BRAF-targeted therapy from second line (BEACON) to first line, combined with FOLFOX — doubling median OS.
Test BRAF up front; a BRAF V600E patient should not start bevacizumab-based chemo alone.
trials.takeaway: First-line encorafenib + cetuximab + FOLFOX doubles OS in BRAF V600E metastatic CRC

trials.name: KEYNOTE-048
trials.descriptor: first-line recurrent/metastatic HNSCC
trials.population: 1L recurrent/metastatic HNSCC (oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, larynx), not curable by local therapy; stratified by PD-L1 CPS
trials.arms: (1) pembrolizumab monotherapy; (2) pembrolizumab + platinum (cis/carbo) + 5-FU; (3) EXTREME = cetuximab + platinum + 5-FU
trials.primary_endpoint: OS + PFS (tested across CPS ≥20, CPS ≥1, total population)
trials.results: Pembro+chemo vs EXTREME OS 13.0 vs 10.7 mo (HR 0.77); CPS≥20 14.7 vs 11.0 (HR 0.60), CPS≥1 13.6 vs 10.4 (HR 0.65). Pembro mono OS: CPS≥20 14.9 vs 10.7 (HR 0.61), CPS≥1 12.3 vs 10.3 (HR 0.78); non-inferior in total population
trials.reference: Burtness B et al. Lancet 2019;394:1915; Harrington KJ et al. JCO 2023 (5-yr)
highlights: Established pembrolizumab-based, CPS-driven therapy as 1L SOC for R/M HNSCC, displacing EXTREME.
CPS ≥1 → pembrolizumab (± chemo); high CPS (≥20) → monotherapy reasonable; CPS <1 → pembro + chemo.
trials.takeaway: Pembrolizumab ± chemo is 1L SOC for R/M HNSCC, chosen by PD-L1 CPS

trials.name: KEYNOTE-689
trials.descriptor: perioperative pembrolizumab, resectable LA HNSCC
trials.population: Newly diagnosed, resectable, locally advanced (stage III/IVA) HNSCC
trials.arms: Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab → surgery → adjuvant pembrolizumab + SOC RT (± cisplatin) → maintenance pembrolizumab, vs SOC alone (surgery + adjuvant RT ± cisplatin)
trials.results: CPS≥10: 3-yr EFS 59.8% vs 45.9% (HR 0.66, p=0.004). CPS≥1: HR 0.70 (p=0.003). Total: HR 0.73 (p=0.008), median EFS 51.8 vs 30.4 mo. ↑ major pathologic response; DMFS 51.8 vs 35.7 mo
trials.reference: Uppaluri R et al. NEJM 2025 (Jun 18); NEJMoa2415434
highlights: First positive perioperative immunotherapy trial in resectable LA HNSCC — establishes neoadjuvant + adjuvant pembrolizumab as a practice-changing new standard.
trials.takeaway: Perioperative pembrolizumab improves EFS in resectable locally advanced HNSCC

trials.name: SWOG 8736
trials.descriptor: CHOP ×3 + involved-field RT vs CHOP ×8 in localized intermediate/high-grade NHL
trials.population: Stage I, IE, or non-bulky II/IIE intermediate- or high-grade NHL (Working Formulation); 401 eligible (200 CHOP+RT, 201 CHOP)
trials.arms: CHOP ×3 → involved-field RT 40-55 Gy vs CHOP ×8 alone
trials.results: 5-yr PFS 77% vs 64% (P=0.03); 5-yr OS 82% vs 72% (P=0.02). Life-threatening toxicity 61/200 vs 80/201 (P=0.06); decreased LVEF in 7 CHOP-alone patients vs 0 (P=0.02). Long-term SWOG follow-up (Stephens, JCO 2016) showed the curves crossing at ~7-9 yr with no lasting advantage
trials.toxicity: Less life-threatening toxicity and no cardiac events with the abbreviated arm
highlights: Established abbreviated chemotherapy + radiation as an option for localized aggressive NHL
Pre-rituximab, and the early PFS/OS advantage did not persist — it no longer defines modern practice
trials.takeaway: Three cycles of CHOP with involved-field RT beat eight cycles of CHOP at 5 years in localized aggressive NHL, but the advantage disappeared with longer follow-up.

trials.name: GELA LNH-98.5
trials.descriptor: R-CHOP vs CHOP in previously untreated DLBCL age 60-80
trials.population: Untreated DLBCL, age 60-80, stage II-IV; 399 randomized (202 R-CHOP, 197 CHOP); 60% aaIPI 2-3
trials.arms: CHOP ×8 q21d vs the same plus rituximab 375 mg/m² on day 1 of each cycle
trials.results: At median 2 yr: CR 76% vs 63% (P=0.005); EFS P<0.001 and OS P=0.007; risk ratio 0.58 (95% CI 0.44-0.77) for treatment failure and 0.64 (0.45-0.89) for death. 10-yr update (Coiffier, Blood 2010;116:2040): PFS 36.5% vs 20%, OS 43.5% vs 27.6%, with equal second cancers and non-lymphoma deaths
trials.toxicity: No clinically relevant increase in toxicity with rituximab, and no excess late toxicity at 10 years
highlights: Established R-CHOP as the global standard of care in DLBCL
An absolute ~16% overall survival gain at 10 years that no chemotherapy backbone has improved on since
trials.takeaway: Adding rituximab to CHOP raised complete response, event-free and overall survival in elderly DLBCL, and the benefit held at ten years.

trials.name: CALGB 50202
trials.descriptor: MT-R induction then EA consolidation, omitting whole-brain radiotherapy, in newly diagnosed PCNSL
trials.population: 44 patients with newly diagnosed primary CNS lymphoma, multicenter
trials.arms: Single arm, two steps: methotrexate 8 g/m² + temozolomide + rituximab induction, then etoposide + cytarabine consolidation in responders. No whole-brain radiotherapy
trials.primary_endpoint: Complete response rate to MT-R induction
trials.results: CR to induction 66%. At median follow-up 4.9 yr, 2-yr PFS 0.57 overall; 2-yr time to progression 0.59 overall and 0.77 among those completing consolidation. Patients over 60 did as well as younger ones; treatment delay was the strongest adverse prognostic variable
trials.toxicity: Dose-intensive consolidation proved feasible outside a single center; myelosuppression predominated
highlights: First multicenter demonstration that dose-intensive consolidation without whole-brain radiotherapy is feasible in PCNSL
Directly motivated CALGB 51101, which randomized this consolidation against autologous transplant
trials.takeaway: MT-R induction with etoposide-cytarabine consolidation achieved outcomes comparable to radiation-containing regimens while sparing the brain from radiotherapy.

trials.name: IELSG32 / MATRix
trials.descriptor: methotrexate/cytarabine ± rituximab ± thiotepa induction in newly diagnosed PCNSL
trials.population: HIV-negative, age 18-70, newly diagnosed PCNSL with measurable disease, ECOG 0-3; 227 enrolled at 53 centers in 5 countries, 219 assessable
trials.arms: 1:1:1 — methotrexate 3.5 g/m² + cytarabine 2 g/m² BID; the same plus rituximab; or the same plus rituximab and thiotepa 30 mg/m² (MATRix). Four courses q21d, then a second randomization to whole-brain radiotherapy or autologous transplant
trials.primary_endpoint: Complete remission rate after induction (first randomization)
trials.results: At median follow-up 30 mo: CR 49% (95% CI 38-60) with MATRix vs 23% (14-31) with methotrexate-cytarabine (HR 0.46, 0.28-0.74) and 30% (21-42) with the rituximab doublet (HR 0.61, 0.40-0.94). Thirteen toxic deaths (6%). Second randomization (Lancet Haematol 2017;4:e510): 2-yr PFS 80% with radiotherapy vs 69% with transplant, HR 1.50, P=0.17 — no significant difference. At 7 years OS was 21% / 37% / 56% across the three induction arms
trials.toxicity: Grade 4 hematologic toxicity most frequent with MATRix; infective complications similar across arms; 6% toxic mortality
trials.reference: Ferreri AJM et al. Lancet Haematol 2016;3:e217
highlights: Established MATRix as the standard induction backbone for PCNSL in patients up to age 70
A randomized phase 2, not a phase 3, and 6% toxic mortality limits its use in frail or older patients
trials.takeaway: Adding rituximab and thiotepa to methotrexate-cytarabine doubled the complete remission rate in PCNSL and made MATRix the standard induction.

trials.name: FLYER
trials.descriptor: 4 cycles R-CHOP + 2 rituximab vs 6 cycles R-CHOP in young favorable-prognosis aggressive B-NHL
trials.population: Age 18-60, stage I-II, normal LDH, ECOG 0-1, no bulk (<7.5 cm), aaIPI 0; 588 in the ITT analysis
trials.arms: R-CHOP ×6 vs CHOP ×4 + rituximab ×6 (4 R-CHOP then 2 rituximab alone), q21d; no planned RT except testicular
trials.results: 3-yr PFS 96% (95% CI 94-99) with 4 cycles vs 93% with 6 — difference +3%, lower bound 0%, non-inferiority met at median follow-up 66 mo. 3-yr OS 99% vs 98%. Adverse events roughly a third lower: 294 hematologic + 1,036 non-hematologic vs 426 + 1,280. Both on-therapy deaths were in the 6-cycle arm
trials.toxicity: Substantially less hematologic and non-hematologic toxicity with 4 cycles
highlights: Made 4×R-CHOP + 2 rituximab standard for young aaIPI-0 non-bulky DLBCL
Applies only to that narrow favorable subset — age ≤60, stage I-II, normal LDH, no bulk
trials.takeaway: Four cycles of R-CHOP plus two extra rituximab doses is non-inferior to six cycles in young favorable-risk DLBCL, with less toxicity.

trials.name: GO29365 (pola-BR)
trials.descriptor: polatuzumab vedotin + bendamustine/rituximab vs bendamustine/rituximab in transplant-ineligible R/R DLBCL
trials.population: Transplant-ineligible R/R DLBCL; randomized cohort of 80 (40 per arm)
trials.arms: Polatuzumab 1.8 mg/kg + bendamustine 90 mg/m² + rituximab 375 mg/m² q21d ×6 vs BR ×6
trials.primary_endpoint: Complete response rate at end of treatment by independent review
trials.results: CR at end of treatment 40.0% vs 17.5% (P=0.026). Median PFS 9.5 vs 3.7 mo, HR 0.36 (95% CI 0.21-0.63), P<0.001; median OS 12.4 vs 4.7 mo, HR 0.42 (0.24-0.75), P=0.002, at median follow-up 22.3 mo. A 106-patient extension cohort gave ORR 41.5%, CR 38.7%
trials.toxicity: Grade 3-4 neutropenia 46.2% vs 33.3%, thrombocytopenia 41% vs 23.1%; peripheral neuropathy 43.6%, grade 1-2 and mostly reversible
highlights: Basis for approval of pola-BR in R/R DLBCL after ≥2 prior lines
Only 40 patients per randomized arm — a very small dataset for a registrational survival claim
trials.takeaway: Adding polatuzumab to bendamustine-rituximab more than doubled complete responses and roughly tripled median survival in transplant-ineligible R/R DLBCL.

trials.name: L-MIND
trials.descriptor: single-arm tafasitamab + lenalidomide in transplant-ineligible relapsed/refractory DLBCL
trials.population: R/R DLBCL after 1-3 prior regimens including an anti-CD20, not ASCT candidates, ECOG 0-2; 81 treated at 35 sites
trials.arms: Single arm: tafasitamab 12 mg/kg IV + lenalidomide 25 mg PO d1-21 for up to 12 cycles, then tafasitamab alone q2wk until progression
trials.primary_endpoint: Best objective response rate by central review
trials.results: Primary (median follow-up 13.2 mo): ORR 60% (95% CI 48-71), CR 43%, PR 18% of 80 evaluable. Five-year final analysis (Duell, Haematologica 2024;109:553): ORR 57.5%, CR 41.3%, median PFS 11.6 mo, median OS 33.5 mo; by prior lines, ORR 67.5% after one line vs 47.5% after ≥2
trials.toxicity: Grade ≥3 neutropenia 48%, thrombocytopenia 17%, febrile neutropenia 12%; serious adverse events 51%
trials.reference: Salles G et al. Lancet Oncol 2020;21:978
highlights: Basis for accelerated approval of tafasitamab + lenalidomide in transplant-ineligible R/R DLBCL
Single-arm phase 2 of 80 patients, enriched for a single prior line — real-world third-line results are lower
trials.takeaway: Tafasitamab plus lenalidomide gave roughly 60% responses and 40% complete responses in transplant-ineligible R/R DLBCL, best after only one prior line.

trials.name: NCI 9177 (risk-adapted DA-EPOCH-R)
trials.descriptor: risk-adapted DA-EPOCH-R in untreated adult Burkitt lymphoma
trials.population: 113 adults with untreated Burkitt lymphoma at 22 centers, any HIV status; 87% high-risk, median age 49, 26% with marrow and/or CSF involvement, 25% HIV-positive
trials.arms: Single arm, risk-adapted: low risk → DA-EPOCH-R ×3 with no CNS prophylaxis; high risk → ×6 with intrathecal methotrexate. No cranial radiation
trials.results: At median follow-up 58.7 mo: EFS 84.5%, OS 87.0%. EFS 100% in low-risk and 82.1% in high-risk, with equivalent outcomes across age, HIV status and IPI. Five treatment-related deaths (4%); febrile neutropenia in 16% of cycles
trials.toxicity: Markedly less toxic than CODOX-M/IVAC or hyper-CVAD; 4% treatment-related mortality
highlights: Made risk-adapted DA-EPOCH-R a standard option for adult Burkitt, including older and HIV-positive patients
Low-risk patients were cured with three cycles and no intrathecal prophylaxis; CSF involvement remains the unsolved problem
trials.takeaway: Risk-adapted DA-EPOCH-R cured about 85% of adults with Burkitt lymphoma regardless of age or HIV status, with far less toxicity than dose-intensive regimens.

trials.name: NP30179 (glofitamab)
trials.descriptor: fixed-duration glofitamab monotherapy after ≥2 prior lines
trials.population: R/R DLBCL with ≥2 prior lines; 155 enrolled, 154 treated; median 3 prior therapies, about a third with prior CAR-T, ~84% refractory to their last regimen
trials.arms: Single arm: obinutuzumab 1,000 mg pretreatment C1D1, glofitamab step-up 2.5 mg C1D8 and 10 mg C1D15, then 30 mg on day 1 of cycles 2-12 — fixed 12 cycles
trials.primary_endpoint: Complete response rate by independent review
trials.results: At median follow-up 12.6 mo: CR 39% (95% CI 32-48), ORR 52%; CR 35% among the 52 with prior CAR-T. Median time to CR 42 days; 78% of complete responses ongoing at 12 mo; 12-mo PFS 37%. Three-year update (Blood 2024): CR 40%, median duration of CR 29.8 mo
trials.toxicity: CRS 63% (grade ≥3 4%), grade ≥3 neurologic events 3%, discontinuation for adverse events 9%
highlights: Basis for approval of glofitamab in R/R DLBCL after ≥2 lines; the fixed 12-cycle course gives treatment-free remission
Obinutuzumab pretreatment is mandatory for CRS mitigation, and CRS is more frequent than with epcoritamab
trials.takeaway: Fixed-duration glofitamab gave a 39% complete response rate in heavily pretreated R/R DLBCL, with most remissions durable off therapy.

trials.name: POLARIX
trials.descriptor: pola-R-CHP vs R-CHOP in previously untreated intermediate/high-risk DLBCL
trials.population: Untreated DLBCL, age 18-80, IPI 2-5; 879 randomized (440 pola-R-CHP, 439 R-CHOP)
trials.arms: 6 cycles pola-R-CHP (polatuzumab replaces vincristine) + 2 rituximab vs 6 cycles R-CHOP + 2 rituximab; double-blind
trials.toxicity: Comparable grade ≥3 adverse events; peripheral neuropathy similar to R-CHOP and largely reversible
highlights: First regimen in two decades to beat R-CHOP on PFS; approved for IPI ≥2 DLBCL
No overall survival benefit; the gains concentrate in age >60, IPI 3-5 and non-GCB disease
trials.takeaway: Pola-R-CHP improved 2-year PFS over R-CHOP in IPI ≥2 DLBCL without any difference in overall survival.

trials.name: EPCORE NHL-1
trials.descriptor: subcutaneous epcoritamab monotherapy after ≥2 prior lines
trials.population: R/R CD20+ large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL, HGBCL, PMBCL, FL grade 3B) with ≥2 prior lines including anti-CD20; n=157, median 3 prior lines, 61.1% primary refractory, 38.9% prior CAR-T
trials.arms: Single arm: subcutaneous epcoritamab with step-up dosing in cycle 1 then 48 mg — weekly cycles 1-3, q2wk cycles 4-9, q4wk from cycle 10, until progression
trials.primary_endpoint: Overall response rate by independent review
trials.results: At median follow-up 10.7 mo: ORR 63.1% (95% CI 55.0-70.6), CR 38.9%; median duration of response 12.0 mo and not reached among complete responders. Two-year update (Leukemia 2024): ORR 63.1%, CR 40.1%, 24-mo PFS 27.8%, OS 44.6%
trials.toxicity: CRS 49.7% (grade 3 only 2.5%), ICANS 6.4% with one fatal event
highlights: Basis for approval of epcoritamab in R/R large B-cell lymphoma after ≥2 lines; the first subcutaneous bispecific in DLBCL
Retains activity after CAR-T, and is dosed continuously rather than for a fixed duration
trials.takeaway: Subcutaneous epcoritamab produced 63% responses and 39% complete responses in heavily pretreated large B-cell lymphoma, including after CAR-T.

trials.name: CALGB 9221
trials.descriptor: azacitidine vs supportive care, first HMA RCT
trials.population: MDS (higher- and lower-risk FAB subtypes)
trials.arms: Azacitidine (75 mg/m²/day SC ×7 days q28d) vs best supportive care (crossover allowed)
trials.results: Higher response (~60% vs 5%) and delayed transformation to AML/death; improved quality of life (OS not significant — crossover)
highlights: The first RCT of azacitidine in MDS → the disease-modifying signal that led to FDA approval (2004).
trials.takeaway: First azacitidine RCT — response and delayed AML transformation; led to FDA approval

trials.name: D-0007
trials.descriptor: Decitabine added to supportive care vs supportive care alone
trials.population: 170 adults with de novo or secondary MDS (IPSS Int-1, Int-2 or high risk); ~70% IPSS Int-2/high risk; CMML included
trials.arms: Decitabine 15 mg/m2 IV over 3 h every 8 h x 3 days (135 mg/m2 per course) every 6 weeks + supportive care vs best supportive care alone
trials.primary_endpoint: Overall response rate (IWG) and time to AML transformation or death
trials.results: ORR 17% with decitabine (9% CR, 8% PR) vs 0% with supportive care (P<.001); a further 13% had hematologic improvement. Median response duration 10.3 months. Time to AML progression or death favored decitabine but was not significant overall: 12.1 vs 7.8 months (P=.16); significant only in subgroups (IPSS Int-2/high 12.0 vs 6.8 months, P=.03). No overall survival benefit was demonstrated. Median exposure was only 3 courses because the protocol withdrew patients after a maintained CR or after 6-8 cycles without response.
trials.toxicity: Myelosuppression: grade 3-4 neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and febrile neutropenia; serious adverse events in 69% of decitabine-treated patients.
highlights: The registration trial that won decitabine FDA approval for MDS in 2006 - it established response and delayed AML transformation, not survival.

Cycle number was capped by protocol design (median 3 courses), the standard explanation for why decitabine underperformed azacitidine; modern practice is at least 4-6 cycles before declaring HMA failure.
trials.takeaway: Decitabine produced real responses (ORR 17% vs 0%) and delayed AML transformation in higher-risk subgroups, but showed no overall survival benefit - in contrast to azacitidine in AZA-001.

trials.name: MDS-003
trials.descriptor: lenalidomide, lower-risk del(5q) MDS
trials.population: Lower/Int-1-risk, transfusion-dependent MDS with del(5q)
trials.arms: Single-arm phase 2 (lenalidomide 10 mg/day)
trials.results: 67% transfusion independence; 73% cytogenetic response (45% complete)
highlights: Established lenalidomide for transfusion-dependent lower-risk del(5q) MDS (FDA approval).
trials.takeaway: Lenalidomide → 67% transfusion independence in lower-risk del(5q) MDS

trials.name: AZA-001
trials.descriptor: azacitidine, higher-risk MDS survival benefit
trials.population: Higher-risk MDS (IPSS Int-2/High; RAEB)
trials.arms: Azacitidine vs conventional care regimens (supportive care, low-dose cytarabine, or intensive chemo — physician's choice)
trials.results: Median OS 24.5 vs 15.0 months (HR 0.58, p<0.001)
trials.reference: Fenaux P et al. Lancet Oncol 2009;10:223
highlights: The practice-defining trial: first to show a survival benefit for a hypomethylating agent in higher-risk MDS.
trials.takeaway: Azacitidine improves OS in higher-risk MDS (24.5 vs 15.0 mo)

trials.name: EORTC 06011
trials.setting: Higher-risk MDS in older adults ineligible for intensive chemotherapy, first line
trials.descriptor: Low-dose decitabine vs best supportive care, powered for overall survival
trials.population: 233 patients age >=60 (median 70) with primary or secondary MDS or CMML, IPSS intermediate or high risk, ineligible for intensive chemotherapy; 53% poor-risk cytogenetics
trials.arms: Decitabine 15 mg/m2 IV over 4 h three times daily x 3 days in 6-week cycles (max 8 cycles) vs best supportive care
trials.results: Primary endpoint NOT met: median OS 10.1 vs 8.5 months, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.66-1.17), P=.38 - no overall survival benefit, in contrast to azacitidine in AZA-001. PFS was prolonged: 6.6 vs 3.0 months, HR 0.68 (0.52-0.88), P=.004. AML-free survival not significant: 8.8 vs 6.1 months, P=.24. AML transformation at 1 year 22% vs 33% (P=.036). CR 13% vs 0%, PR 6% vs 0%, HI 15% vs 2%. Patients received a median of only 4 cycles and ~40% received no more than 2.
trials.toxicity: Grade 3-4 febrile neutropenia 25% vs 7%; grade 3-4 infections 57% vs 52%.
trials.reference: Lubbert M et al. J Clin Oncol 2011;29:1987-96
highlights: The definitive OS-powered test of decitabine against supportive care in higher-risk MDS - and it was negative, which is why azacitidine, not decitabine, is the HMA with a proven survival benefit.
Decitabine still delayed progression and AML transformation and improved quality of life, so it remains reasonable when schedule or tolerability favors it.
trials.takeaway: In older higher-risk MDS, decitabine improved PFS, response and AML transformation but did NOT improve overall survival (10.1 vs 8.5 months, HR 0.88, P=.38) - the key contrast with AZA-001.

trials.name: MDS-004
trials.setting: Lower-risk del(5q) MDS with RBC transfusion dependence
trials.descriptor: Lenalidomide at two dose schedules vs placebo for transfusion independence
trials.population: 205 RBC transfusion-dependent patients with IPSS Low- or Intermediate-1-risk del(5q31) MDS
trials.arms: Lenalidomide 10 mg/day days 1-21 (n=69) vs 5 mg/day days 1-28 (n=69) vs placebo (n=67), 28-day cycles; crossover permitted after 16 weeks
trials.results: RBC-TI >=26 weeks 56.1% (10 mg) and 42.6% (5 mg) vs 5.9% (placebo), both P<.001. Cytogenetic response 50.0% vs 25.0% (P=.066). Pooled lenalidomide 3-year OS 56.5%, 3-year AML risk 25.1%. Achieving RBC-TI >=8 weeks was associated with a 47% reduction in relative risk of death (P=.021) and 42% reduction in risk of AML progression or death (P=.048).
trials.toxicity: Myelosuppression dominates - grade 3-4 neutropenia and thrombocytopenia requiring dose reduction and interruption.
highlights: The randomized placebo-controlled confirmation of lenalidomide in del(5q) MDS, establishing 10 mg days 1-21 as the standard schedule.
Achieving transfusion independence was itself associated with lower risk of death and of AML progression - TI is more than a cosmetic endpoint.
trials.takeaway: Lenalidomide 10 mg (days 1-21) makes roughly half of transfusion-dependent lower-risk del(5q) patients transfusion independent for >=26 weeks, at the cost of significant myelosuppression.

trials.name: MEDALIST
trials.descriptor: luspatercept, lower-risk RS+ MDS after ESA failure
trials.population: Lower-risk, transfusion-dependent MDS with ring sideroblasts / SF3B1, ESA-refractory or -ineligible
trials.arms: Luspatercept vs placebo
trials.results: 38% vs 13% achieved transfusion independence ≥8 wk
highlights: Luspatercept (activin receptor II ligand trap) for RS+ lower-risk MDS after ESA failure (FDA approval).
trials.takeaway: Luspatercept → transfusion independence in RS+ lower-risk MDS after ESA failure

trials.name: BMT CTN 1102
trials.descriptor: Biologic assignment to reduced-intensity allogeneic HCT (donor) vs non-transplant therapy (no donor)
trials.population: 384 patients age 50-75 with de novo MDS that was or had been IPSS Intermediate-2 or high risk; <20% marrow blasts; suitable RIC alloHCT candidates; 34 centers, 2014-2018
trials.arms: Donor arm: reduced-intensity conditioning allogeneic HCT. No-Donor arm: hypomethylating therapy or best supportive care. Assignment was biologic - by availability of an HLA-matched related or unrelated donor within 90 days - not randomized
trials.results: Adjusted 3-year overall survival 47.9% (95% CI 41.3-54.1) in the Donor arm vs 26.6% (95% CI 18.4-35.6) in the No-Donor arm, P=.0001; absolute difference 21.3% (95% CI 10.2-31.8). Three-year leukemia-free survival 35.8% vs 20.6%, P=.003. Benefit seen across all subgroups examined.
trials.reference: Nakamura R et al. J Clin Oncol 2021;39:3328-3339
highlights: The best available evidence that reduced-intensity allogeneic transplant should be offered to fit older adults with higher-risk MDS - a 21-point absolute gain in 3-year survival.
Assignment was by donor availability rather than randomization, which avoids the selection bias of retrospective transplant series while stopping short of a true randomized comparison.
trials.takeaway: Fit patients aged 50-75 with higher-risk MDS who have a matched donor and proceed to RIC allogeneic HCT live substantially longer (3-year OS 47.9% vs 26.6%) - start the donor search at diagnosis.

trials.name: COMMANDS
trials.descriptor: luspatercept vs epoetin alfa, first-line lower-risk MDS
trials.population: Lower-risk, transfusion-dependent MDS, ESA-naive
trials.arms: Luspatercept vs epoetin alfa (head-to-head, first-line)
trials.primary_endpoint: Transfusion independence ≥12 wk + mean Hb rise ≥1.5 g/dL
trials.results: Luspatercept superior: ~59% vs ~31%
highlights: Moved luspatercept to first-line for transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS (beat ESA), regardless of ring-sideroblast status.
trials.takeaway: Luspatercept beats epoetin alfa first-line in transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS

trials.name: IMerge
trials.descriptor: imetelstat, lower-risk MDS after ESA failure
trials.population: Lower-risk, transfusion-dependent MDS, relapsed/refractory to ESAs, non-del(5q)
trials.arms: Imetelstat (telomerase inhibitor) vs placebo
trials.results: 40% vs 15% (8-wk TI); durable responses
highlights: Imetelstat (first-in-class telomerase inhibitor) for ESA-failed lower-risk MDS; FDA-approved 2024 (Rytelo).
trials.takeaway: Imetelstat — telomerase inhibitor for ESA-failed lower-risk MDS (TI 40% vs 15%)

trials.name: VERONA
trials.setting: Treatment-naive intermediate- and higher-risk MDS, first line
trials.descriptor: Adding venetoclax to azacitidine in newly diagnosed higher-risk MDS
trials.population: 509 randomized patients with newly diagnosed MDS, <20% marrow blasts, IPSS-R >3 (intermediate, high or very high); median age 72; prior HMA, therapy-related MDS, MDS/MPN and CMML excluded
trials.arms: Venetoclax 400 mg PO daily days 1-14 + azacitidine 75 mg/m2 on 7 of the first 9 days (n=256) vs placebo + identical azacitidine (n=253), 28-day cycles
trials.results: Primary endpoint NOT met: median OS 22.18 months (95% CI 17.28-27.27) vs 21.68 months (95% CI 17.81-23.79); HR 0.908 (95% CI 0.733-1.126), P=.38 at median follow-up 41.2 months. Secondary endpoints favored the combination: modified ORR 76.2% vs 57.7%; marrow CR 57.8% vs 37.5%; transfusion independence 55.7% vs 33.6% (P=.0003). Subgroup signals in >5% to <20% marrow blasts and in ASXL1, TP53 or RUNX1 mutated disease.
trials.toxicity: No new safety signals. Neutropenia 77.3% vs 60.2%, thrombocytopenia 66.3% vs 58.9%. Dose interruption 78.8% vs 67.9%; azacitidine dose reduction 48.6% vs 27.2%.
trials.reference: Garcia-Manero G et al. SOHO Annual Meeting 2025; abstract MDS-1497
highlights: The largest randomized test of venetoclax in higher-risk MDS - deeper marrow responses and more transfusion independence, but no survival gain, so azacitidine monotherapy remains the standard first-line HMA.
The dissociation between marrow response and survival is the lesson: in MDS, unlike AML, adding venetoclax to an HMA improves depth of response without translating into longer life.
trials.takeaway: Venetoclax added to azacitidine did not prolong overall survival in treatment-naive higher-risk MDS (22.18 vs 21.68 months, HR 0.908, P=.38) despite much higher response rates - not a new standard of care.

trials.name: CheckMate 067
trials.descriptor: nivolumab + ipilimumab vs nivolumab vs ipilimumab
trials.population: Untreated unresectable stage III or IV melanoma
trials.arms: Nivolumab 1 mg/kg + ipilimumab 3 mg/kg × 4 → nivolumab vs nivolumab alone vs ipilimumab alone
trials.primary_endpoint: PFS and OS (combination or nivolumab vs ipilimumab)
trials.results: Primary: PFS 11.5 / 6.9 / 2.9 mo. 10-yr: median OS 72.1 / 36.9 / 19.9 mo; 10-yr OS 43% / 37% / 19%; 10-yr melanoma-specific survival 52% / 44% / 23%; patients progression-free at 3 years had >96% 10-yr MSS
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 59% (combo) vs 24% (nivo) vs 28% (ipi)
trials.reference: Larkin J et al. NEJM 2015;373:23; Wolchok JD et al. NEJM 2025;392:11 (10-yr)
highlights: Ipi/nivo gives the longest survival — roughly half of patients alive at 10 years — at the cost of ~60% grade 3–4 immune toxicity.
Being progression-free at 3 years essentially equals cure; guides the length of surveillance conversations.
trials.takeaway: Nivolumab + ipilimumab yields ~50% 10-year melanoma-specific survival in metastatic melanoma

trials.name: DeCOG-SLT
trials.descriptor: completion lymph node dissection vs observation after positive sentinel node (German trial)
trials.population: Melanoma with sentinel-node metastasis (≤1 mm micrometastasis in 66%), trunk or extremity primary
trials.arms: Complete lymph node dissection vs observation with nodal ultrasound q3mo
trials.results: 3-yr DMFS 77.0% vs 74.9% (NS); 5-yr DMFS, RFS and OS all equivalent; regional recurrence similar
trials.reference: Leiter U et al. Lancet Oncol 2016;17:757; JCO 2019;37:3000 (final)
highlights: With MSLT-II, retired routine completion dissection after a positive sentinel node — nodal ultrasound surveillance is the standard.
Applies mostly to low sentinel-node tumor burden; heavy nodal disease is now managed with neoadjuvant immunotherapy (NADINA).
trials.takeaway: Completion node dissection does not improve DMFS or OS after positive sentinel node (with MSLT-II)

trials.name: CheckMate 238
trials.descriptor: adjuvant nivolumab vs ipilimumab, resected stage IIIB/C–IV
trials.population: Completely resected stage IIIB, IIIC or IV melanoma
trials.arms: Nivolumab 3 mg/kg q2wk vs ipilimumab 10 mg/kg q3wk × 4 then q12wk, each × 1 year
trials.results: 12-mo RFS 70.5% vs 60.8% (HR 0.65); 5-yr RFS 50% vs 39%; 5-yr OS 76% vs 72% (NS); grade 3–4 AEs 14% vs 46%
trials.reference: Weber J et al. NEJM 2017;377:1824; Larkin J et al. Clin Cancer Res 2023 (5-yr)
highlights: Nivolumab beat high-dose ipilimumab on efficacy and toxicity — the trial that retired adjuvant ipilimumab.
Extends adjuvant anti-PD-1 to resected stage IV disease.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant nivolumab beats ipilimumab for RFS with a third of the toxicity in resected stage III–IV melanoma

trials.name: COMBI-AD
trials.descriptor: adjuvant dabrafenib + trametinib, resected stage III BRAF V600E/K
trials.population: Completely resected stage III melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutation
trials.arms: Dabrafenib 150 mg BID + trametinib 2 mg daily × 12 months vs placebo
trials.results: 3-yr RFS 58% vs 39% (HR 0.47); 5-yr RFS 52% vs 36% (HR 0.51); DMFS HR 0.55; OS HR 0.80 (10-yr update, 2024; did not reach significance threshold)
trials.toxicity: Pyrexia (63%), fatigue, nausea; 26% discontinued for AEs
trials.reference: Long GV et al. NEJM 2017;377:1813; Dummer R et al. NEJM 2020 (5-yr)
highlights: The targeted-therapy alternative to anti-PD-1 for resected BRAF-mutant stage III — durable RFS benefit with a plateau after year 3.
Choose vs anti-PD-1 on toxicity profile and patient preference; no head-to-head trial.
trials.takeaway: 12 months of adjuvant dabrafenib + trametinib halves relapse risk in resected BRAF V600 stage III melanoma

trials.name: MSLT-II
trials.descriptor: completion lymph node dissection vs observation after positive sentinel node
trials.population: Melanoma with sentinel-node metastasis
trials.arms: Immediate completion lymph node dissection vs nodal observation with ultrasound
trials.results: 3-yr melanoma-specific survival 86% vs 86% (HR 1.08, NS); regional control better with CLND (92% vs 77%) but no survival benefit; lymphedema 24% vs 6%
highlights: Completion dissection after a positive sentinel node improves regional control but not survival — ultrasound surveillance is now standard (with DeCOG-SLT).
SLNB remains valuable for staging and adjuvant-therapy eligibility.
trials.takeaway: Completion node dissection after positive SLNB does not improve melanoma-specific survival

trials.name: CheckMate 204
trials.descriptor: nivolumab + ipilimumab for melanoma brain metastases
trials.population: Melanoma with ≥1 measurable, untreated brain metastasis (0.5–3 cm); cohort A asymptomatic without steroids, cohort B symptomatic or on steroids
trials.arms: Single-arm: nivolumab 1 mg/kg + ipilimumab 3 mg/kg × 4 → nivolumab 3 mg/kg q2wk
trials.results: Asymptomatic: intracranial ORR 53–57%, 36-mo intracranial PFS ~54%, OS ~72%. Symptomatic/steroids: ORR ~17–22%, 36-mo iPFS ~19%, OS ~37%
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 AEs 55%; CNS events (headache, edema) in ~7%
trials.reference: Tawbi HA et al. NEJM 2018;379:722; Long GV et al. JCO 2023 (3-yr)
highlights: Asymptomatic, steroid-free brain metastases respond to ipi/nivo about as well as extracranial disease — upfront systemic therapy is appropriate, with SRS reserved for residual/oligo lesions.
Steroid dependence is the discriminator: symptomatic patients do poorly on IO and need local therapy ± BRAF/MEK first.
trials.takeaway: Ipi/nivo controls asymptomatic melanoma brain metastases (intracranial ORR >50%); steroid-requiring patients respond poorly

trials.name: KEYNOTE-054 (EORTC 1325)
trials.descriptor: adjuvant pembrolizumab, resected stage III
trials.population: Completely resected stage IIIA (>1 mm nodal metastasis), IIIB or IIIC melanoma
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab 200 mg q3wk × 18 vs placebo (crossover to pembrolizumab at recurrence)
trials.results: 1-yr RFS 75.4% vs 61.0% (HR 0.57); 5-yr RFS 55.4% vs 38.3% (HR 0.61); 5-yr DMFS 60.6% vs 44.5% (HR 0.62); benefit regardless of PD-L1 or BRAF status; OS not significant (crossover)
trials.toxicity: Grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs 14.7%; endocrinopathies
trials.reference: Eggermont AMM et al. NEJM 2018;378:1789; Lancet Oncol 2021 / NEJM Evidence 2022 (5-yr)
highlights: Established adjuvant anti-PD-1 as the standard for resected stage III melanoma, replacing high-dose ipilimumab and interferon.
Now being partly displaced by neoadjuvant IO (NADINA) for macroscopic nodal disease.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant pembrolizumab improves RFS and DMFS in resected stage III melanoma

trials.name: KEYNOTE-716
trials.descriptor: adjuvant pembrolizumab, resected stage IIB/IIC
trials.population: Completely resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma (node-negative, sentinel biopsy negative)
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab 200 mg q3wk × 17 vs placebo
trials.results: 12-mo RFS 90.5% vs 83.1% (HR 0.65 at first interim; 0.61 at second); 3-yr RFS 76.2% vs 63.4% (HR 0.62); DMFS HR 0.59; OS not yet significant
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 17%; permanent endocrinopathies (hypothyroidism ~17%)
trials.reference: Luke JJ et al. Lancet 2022;399:1718; Long GV et al. Lancet Oncol 2023 (DMFS)
highlights: Extends adjuvant anti-PD-1 to node-negative high-risk primaries — RFS and DMFS benefit, but no OS benefit yet, so the conversation is about risk tolerance and irreversible endocrine toxicity.
Stage IIB/IIC recurrence risk rivals stage IIIA/B; SLNB-negative does not mean low risk.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant pembrolizumab improves RFS and DMFS in resected stage IIB/IIC melanoma (no OS benefit yet)

trials.name: RELATIVITY-047
trials.descriptor: nivolumab + relatlimab (anti-LAG-3) vs nivolumab
trials.population: Untreated unresectable or metastatic melanoma
trials.arms: Nivolumab 480 mg + relatlimab 160 mg q4wk (fixed-dose combination) vs nivolumab 480 mg
trials.results: PFS 10.1 vs 4.6 mo (HR 0.75); OS HR 0.80 (NS at analysis); ORR 43% vs 33%
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 19% vs 10% (far below ipi/nivo); adrenal insufficiency and myocarditis slightly increased
highlights: First LAG-3 inhibitor to reach the clinic (Opdualag) — doubles PFS over nivolumab with roughly a third of ipi/nivo's grade 3–4 toxicity.
Reasonable first-line default when ipi/nivo toxicity is a concern; no direct comparison with ipi/nivo exists, and OS benefit was not significant.
trials.takeaway: Nivolumab + relatlimab doubles PFS over nivolumab alone with modest added toxicity

trials.name: CheckMate 76K
trials.descriptor: adjuvant nivolumab, resected stage IIB/IIC
trials.population: Completely resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma
trials.arms: Nivolumab 480 mg q4wk × 12 months vs placebo
trials.results: 12-mo RFS 89% vs 79% (HR 0.42); DMFS HR 0.47; 3-yr RFS HR 0.62 (updated)
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 10%
trials.reference: Kirkwood JM et al. Nat Med 2023;29:2835
highlights: Nivolumab is the alternative to pembrolizumab for stage IIB/IIC; same caveat — no OS benefit demonstrated yet.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant nivolumab reduces recurrence in resected stage IIB/IIC melanoma

trials.name: DREAMseq (ECOG-ACRIN EA6134)
trials.descriptor: immunotherapy-first vs targeted-first sequencing in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma
trials.population: Untreated BRAF V600-mutant metastatic melanoma (asymptomatic brain mets allowed)
trials.arms: Ipilimumab + nivolumab → dabrafenib + trametinib at progression vs dabrafenib + trametinib → ipilimumab + nivolumab
trials.results: 2-yr OS 71.8% vs 51.5% (IO-first vs targeted-first); trial stopped early for benefit; ORR to first-line IO 46%, to first-line BRAF/MEK 43%
highlights: Start with immunotherapy in BRAF-mutant disease — the survival difference comes from durability of IO responses and the poor activity of IO after BRAF/MEK failure.
Exceptions: visceral crisis, symptomatic disease or steroid dependence, where a short BRAF/MEK 'sandwich' buys control first.
trials.takeaway: Ipi/nivo first then BRAF/MEK beats the reverse sequence for OS in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma

trials.name: SECOMBIT
trials.descriptor: sequencing: targeted-first vs IO-first vs 'sandwich' in BRAF-mutant melanoma
trials.population: Untreated BRAF V600-mutant metastatic melanoma
trials.arms: Arm A: encorafenib + binimetinib → ipi/nivo; Arm B: ipi/nivo → encorafenib + binimetinib; Arm C 'sandwich': 8 weeks enco/bini → ipi/nivo → enco/bini at progression
trials.results: 2-yr OS 65% (A, targeted-first) / 73% (B, IO-first) / 69% (C, sandwich); 3-yr OS 54% / 62% / 60%; median OS not reached in any arm; longer follow-up (ASCO 2024 update) continued to favor IO-first and sandwich for PFS and OS
highlights: Concordant with DREAMseq: IO-first or a brief targeted 'sandwich' beats targeted-first for long-term survival.
The sandwich strategy is the evidence base for using BRAF/MEK briefly to debulk symptomatic disease before switching to IO.
trials.takeaway: IO-first or brief targeted 'sandwich' outperforms targeted-first sequencing for OS in BRAF-mutant melanoma

trials.name: SWOG S1801
trials.descriptor: neoadjuvant-adjuvant vs adjuvant-only pembrolizumab
trials.population: Resectable stage IIIB–IV melanoma (measurable disease)
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab 200 mg × 3 pre-op → surgery → 15 adjuvant doses vs surgery → 18 adjuvant doses (same total)
trials.results: 2-yr EFS 72% vs 49% (HR 0.58); no increase in surgical complications; same total pembrolizumab exposure
highlights: Proof that the timing of immunotherapy matters: three doses before surgery, with the tumor and its draining nodes in place, outperform the identical total dose given afterward.
Foundation for NADINA and for neoadjuvant IO as the default in resectable stage III disease.
trials.takeaway: Giving 3 of 18 pembrolizumab doses before surgery improves EFS vs the same doses all after surgery

trials.name: NADINA
trials.descriptor: neoadjuvant ipilimumab + nivolumab vs adjuvant nivolumab, macroscopic stage III
trials.population: Resectable macroscopic stage III melanoma (≥1 pathologically proven lymph node metastasis)
trials.arms: Neoadjuvant ipilimumab 80 mg + nivolumab 240 mg × 2 → TLND; adjuvant nivolumab only if no major pathologic response (or dab/tram if BRAF+) vs upfront TLND → adjuvant nivolumab × 12
trials.results: 12-mo EFS 83.7% vs 57.2% (HR 0.32); major pathologic response 59%; those with MPR had 12-mo RFS 95% — most avoided adjuvant therapy
trials.toxicity: Grade ≥3 systemic AEs 29.7% (neoadjuvant) vs 14.7%
highlights: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy is the new standard for macroscopic stage III melanoma — a huge EFS gain and a response-adapted de-escalation of adjuvant therapy.
The 'flipped' low-dose ipi (1 mg/kg) + nivo (3 mg/kg) × 2 keeps toxicity manageable before surgery.
trials.takeaway: Neoadjuvant ipi/nivo dramatically improves EFS over adjuvant nivolumab in resectable stage III melanoma

trials.name: CYTO-PV
trials.descriptor: hematocrit target <45% vs 45–50% in polycythemia vera
trials.population: JAK2-positive polycythemia vera treated with phlebotomy and/or hydroxyurea
trials.arms: Hematocrit target <45% (low) vs 45–50% (high)
trials.primary_endpoint: Time to cardiovascular death or major thrombosis
trials.results: Primary endpoint 2.7% vs 9.8% (HR 3.91 for the high-hematocrit target); more thromboses and CV events at 45–50%
